name: Great Zimbabwe
info: Great Zimbabwe is the stone-walled city near Masvingo built by ancestral Shona people from the 11th to the 15th century, capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe and the largest of the many 'houses of stone' of southern Africa.

facts.made: Ancestral Shona people, the Karanga, descendants of the Gumanye, who settled the site from around 1000; the stone walls were raised by its ruling dynasty over more than 300 years
facts.form: Three groups of mortarless granite dry-stone walls, the Hill Complex, the Great Enclosure and the Valley Complex, spread over 7.22 square kilometres, the Great Enclosure's walls up to 11 metres high and about 250 metres long around a conical tower
facts.where: In the south-eastern hills of Zimbabwe near Masvingo, a national monument and UNESCO World Heritage Site; most of the soapstone birds are back in Zimbabwe, one remains at Groote Schuur in Cape Town and a soapstone figurine is in the British Museum
facts.known: the Great Enclosure and its Conical Tower; the eight soapstone Zimbabwe Birds; trade in gold and ivory to the Swahili coast; Chinese and Persian imports; the colonial 'Zimbabwe controversy'; the name of the modern state

t: Great Zimbabwe grew rich from cattle and from controlling the trade in gold and ivory between the Zimbabwean Plateau and the Swahili coast.
Power and trade shifted north and west in the 15th and 16th centuries, to Mutapa and Khami, and the city was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century.

Rhodesia's white government pressed archaeologists to deny that black Africans built it; its African origin became the scholarly consensus by the 1950s, and independent Zimbabwe took its name and its bird.
dyk: When the Portuguese captain Vicente Pegado recorded the ruins in 1531, he wrote that 'the natives of the country call these edifices Symbaoe, which according to their language signifies court'.
ev: Ancestral Shona people settled the site
Construction of the stone buildings began, starting with the Hill Complex
The Great Enclosure was begun, and the city became capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe
Great Zimbabwe replaced Mapungubwe as the region's centre of trade
Trade declined, and by the century's end offshoots of the royal family were founding new dynasties
Vicente Pegado, captain of the Portuguese garrison of Sofala, recorded the name Symbaoe
European investigations of the site began, followed by looting by antiquarians from the 1890s to the 1920s
The newly independent country was named after the site and kept the soapstone bird as a national symbol

sections.origins:
The area of Great Zimbabwe was settled by the San long before farming peoples arrived. Bantu-speaking peoples settled there from around 150 BCE, forming agricultural chiefdoms from the 4th century CE. Between the 4th and 7th centuries communities of the Gokomere or Ziwa cultures farmed the valley and mined and worked iron, but built nothing in stone. The later Gumanye people are considered the ancestors of the Karanga, the south-central Shona who would build Great Zimbabwe.

Ancestral Shona people settled the site from around 1000. Agriculture and cattle underpinned a growing social network, and long-distance trade transformed local organisations into regional ones. The ruling dynasty used its wealth to build houses of thick daga, earthen daub, and stone walls to shield itself from public view, a process that advanced rapidly in the 13th century, when Great Zimbabwe became the capital of a kingdom. Its growth has been linked to the decline of Mapungubwe from around 1300, or to the greater availability of gold in its hinterland. The name Zimbabwe may come from Shona dzimba-dze-mabwe, 'large houses of stone', or from dzimba-hwe, 'venerated houses'.
sections.content:
The ruins form three groups. The Hill Complex, the oldest, includes the Eastern Enclosure, where the Zimbabwe Birds are thought to have stood, a high balcony enclosure over it and a huge boulder shaped like the bird. The Great Enclosure has an inner wall circling a series of structures and a younger outer wall, between which stands the Conical Tower, 5.5 metres in diameter and 9 metres high. The Valley Complex is divided into Upper and Lower Valley Ruins. Within the perimeter walls was room for commoners' housing, and dhaka pits served as reservoirs, wells and springs, together able to store more than 18,000 cubic metres of water.

Scholars disagree on what the complexes were for. One view holds that successive kings founded new residences, moving the seat of power from the Hill Complex to the Great Enclosure, the Upper Valley and finally the Lower Valley in the early 16th century. A 'structuralist' view assigns separate functions: rituals, perhaps for rain making, on the hill, the king in the Great Enclosure and citizens in the valley, though some argue the dating of finds does not support it. The Great Enclosure likely served as the royal residence, with public spaces for ritual.
sections.making:
Construction of the stone buildings began in the 11th century and continued for over 300 years. The Hill Complex was occupied from the 11th to 13th centuries, the Great Enclosure, built during the 13th and 14th centuries, from the 13th to 15th, and the Valley Complex from the 14th to 16th. The walls were made of dry stone, set without mortar, and the surviving ruins are built entirely of stone, spanning 730 hectares, an area similar to medieval London. Most people, however, lived in houses of mud on wooden frames, so the stone structures are assumed to have been royal, official or elite buildings.

Population estimates vary: traditional figures put the peak at as many as 18,000 or 20,000 people, while a more recent survey concluded that it likely never exceeded 10,000; no burials have been found to offer another basis. The city was also a centre of gold working. Excavated clay containers, crucibles and tools show gold being heated and turned into wire, beads and ornaments in particular areas of the site, the work of practised artisans rather than a common activity.
sections.reception:
The city's politico-religious ideology legitimised the king, the mambo, by linking rulers, their ancestors and Mwari, God. Great Zimbabwe traded salt, cattle, grain and copper as far north as the Kundelungu Plateau, and much of its wealth came from controlling the routes from the plateau's goldfields to the Swahili coast. Traders travelled the Save and Runde rivers and, through Swahili city-states such as Sofala, sent gold and ivory into the Indian Ocean trade. Chinese pottery, including Longquan stoneware and blue-and-white porcelain of the 14th and 15th centuries, Arabian coins and glass beads reached the city, though there is no evidence of architectural exchange with centres such as Kilwa.

The most important finds are eight birds carved in soapstone on top of monoliths the height of a person, thought to represent the bateleur eagle, in Shona culture a good omen, protective spirit and messenger of god. Pegado's description of 1531 spoke of a 'fortress built of stones of marvelous size' with no mortar. In the 20th century, both colonial and black nationalist writers invoked Great Zimbabwe's past to support their visions of the country, in popular histories and in fiction such as Wilbur Smith's The Sunbird and Stanlake Samkange's Year of the Uprising.
sections.survival:
What ended Great Zimbabwe is unknown. Climate change seems unlikely to have been the main cause, given its favourable rainfall. Shona oral tradition blames a shortage of salt, which may be a figurative way of speaking of depleted land or resources; the aquifer may also have run dry or been contaminated. From the early 15th century a global downturn reduced demand for gold. Korekore tradition says Nyatsimba Mutota of the royal family led people north and founded the Mutapa Empire, and a new trade route along the Zambezi favoured Khami. The site was probably inhabited into the 17th century before it was abandoned.

Investigations began in 1871. European antiquarians looted the site from the 1890s to the 1920s, Richard Nicklin Hall's diggings and gold mining doing much damage and destroying its stratigraphy. Carvings taken around 1890 were sold to Cecil Rhodes; most have since been returned. In the 'Zimbabwe controversy', theories credited Jews, Arabs or Phoenicians with the building, and in the 1960s and 1970s Rhodesia's government censored archaeologists who disputed the official line, until Peter Garlake and Roger Summers left the country. Reconstruction since 1980 and heavy visiting have caused further damage.
sections.legacy:
Great Zimbabwe gave its name to the many smaller zimbabwes, more than 400 sites with monumental mortarless walls across southern Africa, such as Bumbusi in Zimbabwe and Manyikeni in Mozambique. To black nationalists it became a symbol of African achievement, and reclaiming its history was a major aim of those seeking majority rule. In 1980 the newly independent country was named after it, and the soapstone bird, already on the Rhodesian flag and coat of arms, was kept on the new flag; a tower of the site appears on the coat of arms.

Since independence the site has been used to support the ruling party's shifting policies, first as a picture of pre-colonial 'African socialism' in Ken Mufuka's much criticised booklet of 1983, later as a story of wealth gathered by a ruling elite. Local clans, each claiming the site, lament its desecration by antiquarians and archaeologists alike and hold the government responsible for its 'silence' and 'closure'; for many communities it is a living cultural landscape rather than a relic. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a university nearby draws on its history.

summary: Great Zimbabwe, near Masvingo, was built in dry stone by ancestral Shona people from the 11th to the 15th century and grew rich on cattle and the gold trade to the Swahili coast. Abandoned by the 17th century, looted under colonial rule and wrongly credited to outsiders by Rhodesia's government, it gave its name and its bird to independent Zimbabwe.
